title: The first sign (John 2:1–12)
hook: John calls miracles signs: six stone jars of water become the best wine
carry: the best was kept till last

segments.voice: Yesterday, under the fig tree, a skeptic seen before he was met. Your line was can anything good come? What good thing did you find where you didn't expect it? Day five hundred ninety-seven.

A village wedding in Galilee could last for days, and the whole village came. The family's honor rode on the hospitality. Running out of food or wine wasn't just awkward; people would talk about it for years. At a wedding in Cana, it happens. The wine runs out. Jesus is there with his new disciples, and so is his mother. And she's the one who notices. She comes to him and says, simply, in the King James words: "They have no wine." No request. Just the problem, laid in front of her son.

His answer sounds sharp in English: "Woman, what have I to do with thee? mine hour is not yet come." But woman was a respectful way to address a lady in Greek, and he uses the same word for her later, from the cross. His hour is a thread through the whole Gospel: the hour of the cross and glory. And his mother doesn't argue. She turns to the servants: "Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it." Nearby stand six stone water jars, used for the Jewish washing rituals, each holding twenty or thirty gallons. Fill them with water, Jesus says, and they fill them to the brim. Draw some out now, and take it to the master of the feast. He tastes it, has no idea where it came from, and calls over the bridegroom: "Every man at the beginning doth set forth good wine; and when men have well drunk, then that which is worse: but thou hast kept the good wine until now." That's more than a hundred gallons of the best wine at the end of a party. Then John tells us what kind of story this is: "This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee, and manifested forth his glory; and his disciples believed on him." The King James says miracles, but John's Greek word is sēmeion: sign. John never calls Jesus's mighty works by the usual words for power. He calls them signs. A sign isn't the destination; it points beyond itself. Christians have read this one as pointing to abundance, to joy, to a wedding feast at the end of time, to something better saved for last.
screen: then, large: `THOU HAST KEPT THE GOOD WINE UNTIL NOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice something that points beyond itself. Settle, and breathe. Look around wherever you are. Find one ordinary thing: a cup, a ring, a photo, a plant on the windowsill, light on a wall. Let your eyes rest on it. Ask what it points to. A person. A promise. A memory. A hope. Stay with that for a while. Most of what's around us is a sign of something, if we stop long enough to read it. If you pray, you can give thanks for what it points to. The bell holds the time.
Sign. John's word for Jesus's miracles: not just wonders, but things that point beyond themselves to who he is. Cana is the first.
Your line: the best was kept till last. Today, save something good for the end of the day, and give it to someone else. Day five hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Many churches read the wedding at Cana in the weeks after Epiphany, and it is often read at Christian weddings; Catholics pray it as one of the luminous mysteries of the rosary.

original.note: Greek: a sign, a mark, a token. John's word for Jesus's miracles; the root of 'semantics'.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus turned water into wine at a party.
what it means: the first of John's signs, at a wedding, pointing to glory, abundance and the best saved for last.
what a scholar hears: John avoids the Synoptics' usual word for miracles (dynameis, mighty works) and calls them semeia, signs; the jars held perhaps 120 to 180 gallons.

notes: 'Two or three firkins apiece' (John 2:6): about 20–30 gallons each, 120–180 total. Confirm.
John never uses dynamis for Jesus's miracles; he uses semeion and ergon. Confirm.
'Woman' (gynai) as respectful address; used again at John 19:26. Confirm.
Stone jars and purification: the text says 'after the manner of the purifying of the Jews'. Script says 'used for the Jewish washing rituals'. Confirm.
Wedding at Cana as the second luminous mystery (added 2002). Confirm.
The carry has the word 'last' though the KJV has 'until now'; the carry is the index's.
